lds.salvation:
Latter-day Saints speak of salvation in more than one sense. In the broadest sense, because of Jesus Christ every person will be resurrected and thus saved from physical death. In a further sense, salvation means being cleansed from sin through His Atonement and living in a kingdom of glory.

The highest hope is exaltation: to live forever in the celestial kingdom in the presence of Heavenly Father and Jesus Christ, in family relationships that can continue. That blessing comes by the grace of Christ as a person exercises faith, repents, is baptized, receives the gift of the Holy Ghost, and endures in covenants, including those made in the temple.
lds.christian_status:
Members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints identify themselves as Christians. They worship God the Father in the name of Jesus Christ, accept Jesus as the divine Son, the promised Messiah, and the Savior and Redeemer of the world, and take His name upon them at baptism.

They know that other Christians sometimes deny that Latter-day Saints belong under the Christian name, often because of differences about the Godhead, additional scripture, or the Restoration. From inside the faith those differences do not cancel a Christian identity. The Church's own name and its central ordinances all point to Jesus Christ.
lds.trinity:
Latter-day Saints do not use the creedal language of one substance. They speak of the Godhead: God the Eternal Father, His Son Jesus Christ, and the Holy Ghost. These are three distinct beings, united in will, testimony, and purpose so completely that they can be called one God.

The Father and the Son have glorified bodies of flesh and bone. The Holy Ghost is a personage of spirit. This understanding is tied to Joseph Smith's First Vision and to later revelation. Members still pray to the Father in the name of the Son and seek the companionship of the Holy Ghost.
lds.father:
Heavenly Father is the Supreme Being, the literal Father of the spirits of all people, and the God whom Latter-day Saints worship. They also call Him Elohim in some temple and scriptural settings, to distinguish Him from Jehovah, who is identified with the premortal Jesus Christ.

He has a glorified, perfected body of flesh and bone. Members are taught to pray to Him in the name of Jesus Christ. His work and glory is to bring to pass the immortality and eternal life of His children. Jesus Christ and the Holy Ghost are separate from Him, yet perfectly one with Him in the Godhead.
lds.holy_spirit:
Latter-day Saints usually say Holy Ghost for the third member of the Godhead, and Holy Spirit in some scriptural phrasing. He is a personage of spirit, not a mere force, and He does not have a body of flesh and bone. His mission is to testify of the Father and the Son, reveal truth, comfort, and sanctify.

The gift of the Holy Ghost is conferred after baptism by the laying on of hands by those holding Melchizedek Priesthood authority. That gift is the right to His constant companionship so long as a person remains worthy. His influence can be felt before baptism; the gift is a covenant blessing after it.
lds.name_of_god:
Latter-day Saints use several names of God with care. Heavenly Father and God the Father name the Being they worship. In the standard works and in temple contexts, Elohim often refers to the Father, while Jehovah refers to the premortal Jesus Christ, the God of the Old Testament.

Jesus Christ is also Lord, Savior, and Redeemer. Members pray to the Father in the name of Jesus Christ. They do not treat these names as interchangeable persons, but as titles that keep the members of the Godhead distinct while honoring each.
lds.incarnation:
Latter-day Saints teach that Jesus Christ, the Firstborn of the Father in the spirit and the Only Begotten in the flesh, took a mortal body through Mary. That mortal birth is how the premortal Lord entered mortality to work out the Atonement.

He inherited divine power from the Father and mortality from Mary, and so could lay down His life and take it again. Members do not describe this as one person with two natures in creedal wording. They describe a divine Son who truly became man, lived sinlessly, suffered, died, and rose with a glorified body.
lds.natures_of_christ:
Jesus Christ is a distinct divine Being who is literally the Son of God. In mortality He had a body subject to pain and death, yet He was the Jehovah of the Old Testament and remained without sin. After the Resurrection He has a glorified, immortal body of flesh and bone, as the Father does.

This is not the language of Chalcedon or of miaphysite formulas. The emphasis is personal and narrative: who He is in the plan of salvation, what He did in Gethsemane and on the cross, and that He lives now as a resurrected God, separate from the Father and one with Him in purpose.
lds.virgin_birth:
Latter-day Saints accept the virgin birth. Jesus was conceived by the power of God, and Mary was His mother in the flesh while remaining a virgin at His birth. He is the Only Begotten of the Father in the flesh.

Beyond that central claim, members do not usually dwell on philosophical details of the conception. Mary is honored as the chosen mother of the Son of God. The point of the teaching is that Jesus is truly the Father's Son and truly mortal through His mother.
lds.preexistence_of_christ:
Jesus Christ lived as a spirit before His birth, as all people did. In that premortal life He was the Firstborn of the Father, the Beloved Son who volunteered to be the Savior when the Father presented the plan of salvation.

Latter-day Saints identify the premortal Christ with Jehovah, the God who spoke with prophets and led Israel. He created the earth under the Father's direction. Preexistence here is not only His. Every human spirit is a child of Heavenly Father and lived with Him before coming to earth.
lds.atonement:
The Atonement of Jesus Christ is the center of the plan of salvation. Latter-day Saints teach that He suffered for the sins, pains, and infirmities of all people, beginning in Gethsemane and completed on the cross, and that He died and rose again.

Because of that offering, all will be resurrected, and all who repent and come to Him can be forgiven and changed. His grace is not a reward that ignores covenants, and covenants have no power without His Atonement. Members speak of applying the Atonement in daily repentance, healing, and hope of exaltation.
lds.resurrection_of_christ:
Latter-day Saints teach that Jesus Christ rose from the tomb with a tangible, immortal body of flesh and bone. Witnesses in the New Testament and in the Book of Mormon, including His appearance to the people at the temple in Bountiful, are read as historical.

His resurrection is the firstfruits and the guarantee that every person will be resurrected. It also shows the kind of glorified body the Father and the Son possess. Easter is kept as a witness that He lives, not only as a symbol of spring or of spiritual renewal.
lds.ascension:
After His resurrection Jesus ministered for a time and then ascended to the Father, as the New Testament describes. Latter-day Saints add that He has appeared again in this dispensation, including to Joseph Smith, and that He will return in glory.

The ascension does not mean He became only a spirit. He remains a resurrected, embodied Son at the right hand of the Father, directing His work through living prophets and through the Holy Ghost.
lds.offices_of_christ:
Jesus Christ is Creator, Jehovah of the Old Testament, Savior and Redeemer, Judge, and the head of His Church. He is the Firstborn and the Only Begotten, the Mediator with the Father, and the Bridegroom of the Church.

Latter-day Saints do not usually arrange these roles into the Protestant threefold office of prophet, priest, and king as a formal scheme, but they recognize Him as the great Prophet, the High Priest of our profession, and the Lord who will reign as King in the Millennium.
lds.gifts_of_the_spirit:
Gifts of the Spirit are blessings the Holy Ghost gives for the benefit of the Church and of individuals. They include faith, healing, prophecy, tongues, interpretation, revelation, wisdom, knowledge, and others named in scripture, including the Book of Mormon and the Doctrine and Covenants.

These gifts are expected to continue. They are sought with humility and are tested against scripture and priesthood order. Not every spiritual impression is a gift to be announced publicly. The most needful gifts are those that lead a person to Christ and to keep covenants.
lds.baptism_in_the_spirit:
Latter-day Saints speak of the baptism of fire and of the Holy Ghost. After water baptism, a person may receive the gift of the Holy Ghost by the laying on of hands. That ordinance invites a sanctifying, purifying influence sometimes called the baptism of fire.

It is not identical with speaking in tongues as a required sign. The promised companionship of the Holy Ghost is the standing gift. Occasions of especially strong spiritual confirmation are welcomed, but the covenant pattern is baptism by water and then by the Spirit through authorized hands.
lds.justification:
Justification, in Latter-day Saint teaching, is being made right with God through the Atonement of Christ as a person exercises faith, repents, and enters the gospel covenant. It is not described as a one-time legal fiction that leaves the person unchanged.

Being justified and becoming sanctified belong together in the path of discipleship. Baptism is for the remission of sins. Continuing repentance and the Holy Ghost keep a person in that justified standing. Final judgment will still look at what one has become by the grace of Christ.
lds.sanctification:
Sanctification is the process of being made clean, holy, and more like Christ through His blood and the Holy Ghost. It follows faith, repentance, and the ordinances of the gospel and continues as a person yields to the Spirit.

Latter-day Saints do not usually isolate sanctification as a second work separate from justification in Holiness-movement terms. They do teach that a disciple can be filled with the Spirit, purified, and eventually prepared for the presence of God. Temple covenants and daily repentance are part of that path.
lds.glorification:
What many Christians call glorification, Latter-day Saints most often call exaltation or eternal life in its fullest sense: to live in the highest degree of the celestial kingdom, in the presence of the Father and the Son, with a glorified body, and, for those sealed in the new and everlasting covenant of marriage, in an eternal family.

Resurrection itself is a kind of glory given to all. The kingdoms of glory differ. Exaltation is not automatic. It is the promised fullness for those who receive Christ and keep the covenants He has offered.
lds.theosis:
Latter-day Saints teach that God's children may become like Him. That hope is usually named exaltation rather than theosis. Through the Atonement and by keeping covenants, men and women may receive a fullness of joy, a glorified body, and, in the highest degree of the celestial kingdom, the continuation of the family and a share in the kind of life God lives.

This is not a claim that creatures become the same Being as the Father, or that they stop worshipping Him. He remains God. The teaching is familial: children growing up unto the stature of their Father by the grace of Christ.
lds.grace:
Grace is the enabling and saving power that comes from Jesus Christ. Latter-day Saints teach that no one earns resurrection or forgiveness. His grace makes both possible. A much-quoted Book of Mormon phrase says people are saved by grace after all they can do.

Members debate how to weigh that phrase. Official teaching in recent generations stresses that grace is not a wage paid after perfect performance. People are to do all they can—faith, repentance, ordinances, enduring—while relying wholly on Christ, who is able to make weak things strong. Works without His grace cannot save; grace without a willing heart is not the path He taught.
lds.faith_and_works:
Faith in Jesus Christ is the first principle of the gospel. It is meant to lead to repentance, baptism, the gift of the Holy Ghost, and enduring to the end. Works are the lived covenant, not a separate ladder beside grace.

Latter-day Saints reject both the idea that any mortal checklist replaces the Atonement and the idea that a confessed faith can remain fruitless and still fulfill the gospel. They read James and the Book of Mormon together on this point: faith without works is dead, and works without Christ have no saving power.
lds.election:
Latter-day Saints speak of election and of foreordination more than of unconditional election. In the premortal life God chose and foreordained some to particular missions, knowing their character and His purposes. That is not the same as forcing a mortal outcome.

Making one's calling and election sure is a scriptural phrase some members use for a sealing promise of eternal life given to the fully faithful. It is not treated as casual or as a substitute for enduring. Agency remains. A premortal appointment does not remove the need to choose Christ in this life.
lds.perseverance:
Latter-day Saints say endure to the end. Baptism and a testimony do not make later unfaithfulness impossible. A person can fall from fellowship and from promised blessings, and can also repent and return.

Covenants are meant to hold a person in the way. Temple recommends, the sacrament, and continuing repentance are how members stay in the covenant. Final salvation in the highest sense is not treated as an irreversible status given at a single moment of decision in youth.
lds.repentance:
Repentance is a principle of the gospel, not only a crisis at conversion. It includes recognizing sin, feeling godly sorrow, confessing where needed, forsaking the sin, making restitution when possible, and turning to Christ.

Serious sins may require confession to a bishop. Everyday repentance is expected of every disciple. Because of the Atonement, repentance is a gift, not a humiliation. The aim is change of heart and reconciliation with God, not mere penalty management.
lds.original_sin:
Latter-day Saints do not teach that children inherit guilt from Adam. The second Article of Faith says people will be punished for their own sins, not for Adam's transgression. The Fall is still real and necessary. It brought mortality, opposition, and the conditions in which agency and the Atonement operate.

Adam and Eve are honored for stepping into mortality. Little children are innocent through Christ's Atonement and are not baptized until the age of accountability, taught as eight years. Human beings have a fallen nature and also remain children of God.
lds.human_nature:
A human being is a spirit child of Heavenly Parents, clothed in a mortal body. The natural man is an enemy to God unless he yields to the Holy Ghost. That phrase names the fallen, selfish pull of mortality, not the destruction of the divine lineage.

People are capable of good and of sin. They need the Atonement, not because they are worthless, but because they cannot fulfill the plan without Christ. The body is a gift, not a prison. Resurrection will restore it in glory.
lds.image_of_god:
Latter-day Saints take the image of God in a strong sense. Human beings are of God's family. Male and female were created in His image, and the Father and the Son have glorified bodies. People are spirit sons and daughters who can, by grace, grow to become like their Father.

This does not make mortals His equals now. It explains why the plan is familial rather than merely legal, and why the body matters. Gender is taught as part of that eternal identity in current official statements, though members sometimes discuss how to apply that teaching.
lds.free_will:
Agency is a central Latter-day Saint word. In the premortal world a plan that preserved agency was chosen, and a plan that would have forced righteousness was rejected. In mortality people remain free to choose liberty and eternal life or captivity and death, in Lehi's language.

Agency does not mean God never constrains circumstances, or that grace is unnecessary. It means accountability is real and coercion is contrary to the plan. Even covenant life is entered and kept by choice.
lds.scripture:
The standard works are the open scriptural canon used in the Church: the Bible (Latter-day Saints commonly use the King James Version in English), the Book of Mormon, the Doctrine and Covenants, and the Pearl of Great Price.

All of these are received as the word of God, with the Book of Mormon called the keystone. The Bible is believed to be the word of God as far as it is translated correctly. Living prophets can add scripture. Personal revelation is expected, but it is not added to the standard works without the order of the Church.
lds.canon:
Latter-day Saints have an open canon. The standard works can receive additions when the Church, under the President of the Church, accepts new revelation as scripture, as happened with official declarations and with sections of the Doctrine and Covenants.

The Book of Mormon is not a replacement Bible. It is another testament of Jesus Christ, standing with the Bible. Closed-canon churches often see this as the decisive break. Inside the faith it is the expected fruit of a living Church.
lds.inspiration:
Scripture is inspired of God. Prophets write as moved upon by the Holy Ghost. Latter-day Saints also allow that ancient records can be copied, abridged, and translated, and that some biblical passages may not have been transmitted perfectly.

Inspiration is not limited to the written past. The same Spirit that inspired scripture can inspire living apostles and personal guidance, which is then weighed against the standard works and the united voice of the First Presidency and the Twelve.
lds.open_canon:
An open canon means God has not stopped speaking. The Book of Mormon, Doctrine and Covenants, and Pearl of Great Price sit beside the Bible as scripture. Further revelation can be added when it comes through the President of the Church and is presented to the Saints.

This is why members invite others to read the Book of Mormon and pray about it. The question is not whether the Bible is enough as a witness of Christ. It is whether God may still give scripture in a new dispensation.
lds.continuing_revelation:
Continuing revelation is the claim that God still speaks through living prophets and apostles, and also to individuals for their own lives. The President of the Church is sustained as prophet, seer, and revelator. The Twelve share in that apostolic witness.

Public, binding revelation for the whole Church comes in a set order. Personal revelation does not authorize someone to announce new doctrine for the Church. Members expect the Spirit to confirm teaching, warn, comfort, and direct, in harmony with existing scripture.
lds.apostolic_succession:
Latter-day Saints do not trace priesthood through an unbroken line of bishops from the first century. They teach that authority was lost in the Great Apostasy and restored by heavenly messengers to Joseph Smith, including Peter, James, and John, who conferred the Melchizedek Priesthood.

Succession since then follows the Quorum of the Twelve. When the President of the Church dies, the First Presidency is dissolved and the senior apostle becomes President. That is their form of apostolic succession: restored keys handed on by living apostles.
lds.prophetic_authority:
The living prophet is the President of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Members sustain him and the Twelve as prophets, seers, and revelators. His office is to hold all restored priesthood keys and to speak for the Lord to the Church.

Earlier prophets, including Joseph Smith and those in the Bible and Book of Mormon, are honored, but they do not outrank the living prophet in directing the present Church. Members are taught to receive his counsel with the Spirit, not as a replacement for personal agency.
lds.priesthood_authority:
Priesthood is the authority and power of God delegated to man to act for the salvation of God's children. In the Church it is organized as the Aaronic Priesthood and the Melchizedek Priesthood. Keys are the right to direct that authority and are held by designated leaders, with all keys resting in the President of the Church.

Worthy men and boys are ordained to priesthood offices. Priesthood blessings, ordinances, and power in covenant life are taught as available to women and men alike. Women are not ordained to those offices, a point some members continue to discuss while official teaching remains as stated.
lds.church:
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints is understood as the restored Church of Jesus Christ, organized again in 1830 with apostles, prophets, and priesthood keys. It is both a worldwide institution and a covenant people.

Local life is in wards and branches, gathered into stakes. The Church administers ordinances, teaches doctrine, and offers a community of Saints. It does not claim that only its members are decent people, or that God never inspires anyone else. It does claim unique restored authority.
lds.one_true_church:
A founding revelation speaks of the Church as the only true and living church upon the face of the whole earth, with which the Lord was well pleased, speaking to the Church as a whole. Members hear that as a claim about restored priesthood keys, ordinances, and revelation, not as a claim that every other believer's faith is empty.

The phrase is blunt, and outsiders often hear it as arrogance. Inside the faith it names a duty: this Church must offer the ordinances of salvation and keep itself living by continuing revelation.
lds.great_apostasy:
The Great Apostasy is the belief that after the death of the apostles the Church lost priesthood keys, saving ordinances in their fullness, and the unified direction of living apostles. Plain and precious things were also lost or altered in the record of scripture.

This is why a Restoration, not only a Reformation, was needed. Reformers are often spoken of with respect as preparing a world that could receive new revelation. The apostasy claim is about authority and fullness, not about the disappearance of all Christian faith or virtue.
lds.church_discipline:
When a member's standing is in question because of serious sin or apostasy, a membership council may be held under priesthood direction. Possible outcomes include no action, restrictions, withdrawal of membership, or, in older language, excommunication.

The stated purposes are to protect others, to help the person repent, and to keep the name of the Church clear. Confidentiality and an invitation to return after repentance are part of current handbook practice. Informal counsel from a bishop handles many matters short of a council.
lds.restoration:
The Restoration is the return of the gospel of Jesus Christ, priesthood authority, and the Church itself through the Prophet Joseph Smith, beginning with the First Vision and including new scripture, the coming of heavenly messengers, and the organization of the Church in 1830.

It is not only a historical event. Members speak of an ongoing Restoration, with further light, temples, and worldwide gathering still underway. The Restoration answers the Great Apostasy and is the reason the Church exists in its present form.
lds.ordination:
Ordination is the laying on of hands by those in authority to confer a priesthood office, such as deacon, teacher, priest, elder, or high priest. Setting apart is a related blessing that authorizes a person, woman or man, to serve in a calling without conferring a priesthood office.

Both are done in the name of Jesus Christ and are recorded. Authority to ordain traces to restored keys. A sincere desire to serve does not replace that line of authorization.
lds.priesthood:
Priesthood names both God's power and the authorized means by which ordinances are performed in the Church. The Aaronic Priesthood concerns preparatory ordinances such as baptism and the sacrament. The Melchizedek Priesthood concerns the higher ordinances, including confirmation, endowment, sealing, and governing the Church.

Men are ordained to offices in these priesthoods. Official teaching also says that women who receive temple ordinances and serve in callings under keys exercise priesthood authority in those assignments and have access to priesthood power by keeping covenants. They are not ordained to the offices themselves.
lds.elders:
Elder is a Melchizedek Priesthood office. Men ordained elders may confirm, bless the sick, confer the gift of the Holy Ghost, and officiate in other ordinances as authorized. Full-time missionaries are commonly called elders or sisters as courtesy titles.

Members of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles and some other General Authorities are also addressed as Elder. The word therefore names both a local office and an apostolic style of address. It is not the same as a Protestant ruling elder.
lds.deacons:
Deacon is the first office in the Aaronic Priesthood, usually conferred on worthy young men beginning at age eleven or twelve under current policy. Deacons pass the sacrament and assist in other temporal and meetinghouse duties.

The office is preparatory. It is not a board of financial officers as in some Protestant congregations, though adult Aaronic Priesthood holders may serve if they have not been ordained elders. The pattern is biblical in name and Restorationist in practice.
lds.priesthood_of_believers:
Latter-day Saints do not use priesthood of all believers as their main slogan. They teach that every accountable person should receive saving ordinances and that priesthood power and blessings reach women and men through covenants.

They do not conclude from this that every member may baptize or preside without ordination or keys. Authority to administer ordinances is given in an ordered way. The contrast with Protestant usage is real: access to God's power is wide; the right to perform specific ordinances is not simply self-claimed.
lds.apostles_today:
The Church is led by a First Presidency and a Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, sustained as prophets, seers, and revelators. Apostles are special witnesses of Jesus Christ in all the world. When one dies, another is called by revelation through the President of the Church.

This is not a metaphorical apostleship. Members believe these men hold the same restored keys that Peter, James, and John conferred. Other Christian bodies that say the apostolic age ended hear this as a grave claim. Inside the faith it is the ordinary government of the Church.
lds.baptism:
Baptism is by immersion, performed by someone holding proper priesthood authority, in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost. It is for the remission of sins and is the gate into the Church and the covenant path. It is offered to those who have reached the age of accountability and are capable of repentance, not to infants.

Baptism must be followed by confirmation and the gift of the Holy Ghost. Vicarious baptism for the dead is performed in temples so that those who died without the ordinance may accept it in the spirit world. Without authority, the form alone is not accepted as the restored ordinance.
lds.matrimony:
Marriage performed by civil or parish authority is honored, but the Church's distinctive hope is temple marriage, a sealing that can bind a husband and wife, and their children, beyond death if they remain faithful.

A sealing is an ordinance of the Melchizedek Priesthood, received in a temple by those who hold a recommend. Those married civilly first may later be sealed. The rite is not only a blessing of a contract. It is entrance into the new and everlasting covenant of marriage, required for exaltation in the highest celestial degree.
lds.sacraments:
Latter-day Saints usually say ordinances rather than sacraments. Saving ordinances include baptism, confirmation, ordination to the Melchizedek Priesthood for men, the temple endowment, and sealing. The sacrament of the Lord's Supper is blessed and passed each Sunday as a renewal of baptismal covenants.

Ordinances require authority and a prescribed wording or pattern. They are channels of covenant, not magic. The sacrament uses bread and water. Worthiness to partake is a matter of repentance and standing in the Church.
lds.temples:
A temple is a house of the Lord, distinct from a meetinghouse. In temples, Latter-day Saints receive the endowment, are sealed as families, and perform vicarious ordinances for the dead, including baptism and endowment.

Entry requires a recommend, obtained through interviews about faith and conduct. The endowment teaches the plan of salvation and includes covenants of obedience, sacrifice, the gospel, chastity, and consecration. Members speak of these things with restraint outside the temple. Temples express the belief that God's work reaches both sides of the veil.
lds.prayer:
Prayer is addressed to Heavenly Father in the name of Jesus Christ. Members are taught to give thanks, ask for what is needed, seek forgiveness, and listen. Family prayer, personal prayer, and prayer over meals and over the sacrament are ordinary.

Public prayers in meetings follow that same pattern. Members do not pray to Mary, to saints, or to the dead. They may ask the Father about the truth of the Book of Mormon and about personal decisions, expecting the Holy Ghost to answer in mind and heart.
lds.sabbath:
The Sabbath day is kept on Sunday in most of the Church, as the Lord's day of resurrection, except in a few places where local custom and Church direction use another day. It is a day for worship, sacrament meeting, rest from ordinary work and commerce, and family or ministering service.

Members vary in how strictly they apply the counsel. Official teaching still asks them to set the day apart, prepare beforehand, and keep it a sign of the covenant, not an empty list of bans.
lds.fasting:
On the first Sunday of the month, in ordinary practice, members go without food and drink for about two meals, pray, and give a fast offering for the poor. That day includes a fast and testimony meeting.

Private fasts are also encouraged when seeking guidance, healing, or help for others. Those who cannot fast from food for health reasons are not condemned. The point is to humble the soul and to join prayer with sacrifice.
lds.mary:
Mary is honored as the mother of Jesus Christ, chosen and highly favored, a virgin who brought the Son of God into mortality. Latter-day Saints retell the Nativity with reverence and name her in the Gospels and in the Book of Mormon prophecy of a virgin at Nazareth.

She is not prayed to, and she is not placed at the center of devotion. Official teaching does not define an Immaculate Conception or Assumption as Catholic dogma does. Honor is real; worship belongs to the Father and the Son.
lds.intercession_of_saints:
Latter-day Saints pray only to the Father in the name of Jesus Christ. They do not ask Mary or departed Saints to intercede. Jesus Christ is the Mediator.

They do believe that the dead in Christ continue in the work of the Lord in the spirit world, and that priesthood keys and sealing join the human family. That is not the same as a cult of the saints. Names of righteous dead are remembered with thanks, not invoked as helpers in prayer.
lds.prayers_for_the_dead:
Rather than prayers that shorten punishment, Latter-day Saints perform ordinances for the dead in temples, especially baptism for the dead, confirmation, endowment, and sealing. The person in the spirit world may accept or reject the ordinance.

This rests on the belief that the gospel is preached to the dead and that God is just toward those who never heard it in mortality. Genealogical work feeds that temple work. Members also pray for living and dead loved ones in the ordinary sense of commending them to God, but the distinctive practice is vicarious ordinance work.
lds.heaven:
Heaven, in ordinary speech, means living again in God's presence. In more precise teaching, almost all people are heirs of some kingdom of glory after resurrection: celestial, terrestrial, or telestial. The celestial kingdom itself has degrees. The highest is exaltation with the Father.

A very small number who become sons of perdition are not heirs of a kingdom of glory. Heaven is therefore not a single identical reward. It is a set of gracious outcomes that still honor agency and covenant.
lds.hell:
Hell can mean the misery of spirit prison before resurrection, where the unrepentant suffer and the gospel is still offered. It can also mean the final state of sons of perdition, sometimes called outer darkness, after the resurrection and judgment.

It does not usually mean that the mass of humankind is endlessly tortured. Most who suffer in spirit prison are understood to be resurrected to a kingdom of glory. Outer darkness is taught as rare, reserved for those who sin against a fullness of light.
lds.intermediate_state:
Between death and resurrection, spirits live in the spirit world, divided in prophetic description between paradise and prison. The righteous rest from care and continue the Lord's work. Those who did not know the gospel, or who rejected it, may be taught and may repent.

This state is conscious. Latter-day Saints do not teach soul sleep. Temple work on earth corresponds to preaching and choice on that side of the veil. Resurrection and judgment still lie ahead.
lds.resurrection_of_the_dead:
Every person who has lived will be resurrected with an immortal body because of Jesus Christ. The resurrection of the just and of the unjust differs in timing and in glory, but none is left a spirit forever.

Resurrected bodies are real. The Savior's risen body is the pattern. For Latter-day Saints this is why cremation debates and funeral forms matter less than the promise that the spirit and body will be reunited, never again to be divided.
lds.last_judgment:
After the Resurrection comes final judgment, when all are assigned to a kingdom of glory or, for a few, to outer darkness. Jesus Christ is the Judge. Records, works, desires, and the use made of light and ordinances enter into that judgment.

An earlier, related teaching is that a person begins to face the consequences of choices already in this life and in the spirit world. The last judgment still settles the everlasting inheritance. Mercy in Christ and justice are both affirmed.
lds.second_coming:
Jesus Christ will return in power and glory, end wickedness, and begin His millennial reign. Latter-day Saints watch for signs but are cautioned against setting dates. The gathering of Israel, the building of temples, and the preaching of the gospel are part of the preparation.

The Second Coming is personal and public, not only inward. It is tied to the restoration of Israel and to the earth receiving its paradisiacal glory. Members are told to be ready rather than alarmed.
lds.millennium:
The Millennium is a thousand years when Christ will reign on the earth. Satan will be bound, peace will spread, and temple work and teaching will continue for those who need ordinances and knowledge.

Resurrection of the just is associated with His coming. At the end of the thousand years there will be a last uprising and then the final judgment. The teaching is premillennial in outline: Christ returns before that era of peace, not after the world perfects itself.
lds.degrees_of_glory:
Doctrine and Covenants 76 describes three degrees of glory: celestial, terrestrial, and telestial, compared to the sun, moon, and stars. The celestial kingdom is the presence of the Father and the Son. Within it, the highest degree requires the new and everlasting covenant of marriage.

This vision comforts members about the fate of the many who do not receive a fullness in this life. It also refuses a simple two-room afterlife of only heaven and hell. Glory differs, and yet almost all are saved from endless torment.
lds.spirit_world:
The spirit world is where the dead live until resurrection. Prophetic teaching divides it into spirit paradise and spirit prison. Missionary work continues there. Ordinances performed on earth by proxy can be accepted there.

Family ties, memory, and moral agency continue. The spirit world is not a metaphor for being forgotten, and it is not reincarnation. It is the next room in the plan of salvation, still under the lordship of Christ.
lds.new_creation:
After the Millennium and the last judgment the earth will be renewed and receive its celestial glory. The meek shall inherit a sanctified earth. That hope sits beside the hope of a place in the Father's kingdom.

Latter-day Saints therefore care about the earth as a planned creation, not as a disposable stage only. The new earth is connected to the same world people now walk, glorified rather than thrown away.
lds.marriage:
Marriage between a man and a woman is ordained of God. The highest form is eternal marriage, a temple sealing that can last beyond death. Official teaching presently defines marriage as between a man and a woman, while asking members to be kind to those who disagree or who are not married.

Not all faithful members are married in this life. The Church teaches that no blessing will be denied the righteous who were denied a fair chance here. Still, the doctrine of exaltation is framed in family language, which is why marriage is not treated as only a private contract.
lds.divorce:
Civil divorce is recognized as a painful legal fact. A temple sealing is not automatically canceled by civil divorce. A cancellation of sealing is a separate process under the First Presidency.

Members who divorce may remain in full fellowship depending on circumstances. Remarriage in the temple, when a prior sealing exists, requires authorization. The ideal is an enduring covenant; the practice admits that some marriages fail and that pastoral judgment is needed.
lds.sexual_ethics:
The law of chastity requires sexual relations only between a husband and wife, lawfully married. Pornography, adultery, fornication, and other sexual sins are taught as needing repentance. Same-sex marriage is not performed or recognized as a temple covenant in current official teaching.

Application to same-sex attracted members has shifted in handbook details over time, and members are not of one mind about tone and policy. The standing doctrinal sentence remains the law of chastity within heterosexual marriage, together with a call to treat every person as a child of God.
lds.tithing:
Tithing is a tenth of one's increase, paid to the Church. It is a commandment and a covenant practice, taught from the Old Testament and from latter-day revelation. Honest tithe paying is required for a temple recommend.

Fast offerings and other humanitarian or missionary giving are separate. Members decide what 'increase' means in edge cases with their own conscience and, if needed, a bishop's counsel. The promised blessing is both spiritual and, in Malachi's language, temporal.
lds.alcohol:
The Word of Wisdom, a health revelation in the Doctrine and Covenants, directs members to abstain from alcohol, tobacco, coffee, and tea, and to use wisdom in eating. It is now a commandment for temple worthiness, though it was first given as counsel.

Obedience is a marker of discipleship in the modern Church. The revelation also praises wholesome herbs and grains and cautions about too much meat. Members differ about cola drinks and other details; the clear prohibitions are taught uniformly.
lds.church_and_state:
The Church claims political neutrality as an institution and does not endorse candidates. The twelfth Article of Faith affirms honoring the law of the land. Members are encouraged to vote and to serve in civic life according to conscience.

In a few moral questions the Church sometimes speaks in the public square. That tension is acknowledged. The ideal remains a free exercise of religion without the Church becoming a party, and without the state running the Church.
lds.food_laws:
Dietary teaching is mainly the Word of Wisdom: no alcohol, tobacco, coffee, or tea, with counsel about eating wholesome food and using meat sparingly. It is not a full kosher or Adventist unclean-meats code, though some members eat little meat and avoid stimulants beyond the listed drinks.

Blood as food is not a central Latter-day Saint issue. The Word of Wisdom is received as revelation for this dispensation, a temporal commandment with spiritual promises, including wisdom and health.
lds.ordination_of_women:
Men are ordained to priesthood offices. Women are not ordained to those offices in current Church government. Official teaching adds that women receive priesthood power through covenants, serve with priesthood authority in callings issued under keys, officiate in certain temple ordinances, and are essential to the work.

Some members accept that arrangement as revealed and sufficient. Others hope for change. The living prophet and the Twelve set the practice. The conversation inside the Church is real, but it has not altered the rule of ordination itself.
lds.headship:
In the family a husband and wife are taught to be equal partners. A father who holds the Melchizedek Priesthood is also taught to preside in righteousness, which official voices explain as serving, not ruling. Presiding in the home is the usual phrase.

How that pair of sentences—'equal partners' and 'preside'—fits together is discussed among members. Abuse is condemned. Decision-making is supposed to be unified and kind. The sealing ordinance binds man and woman together rather than ranking one as the other's God.
lds.mormon_label:
The Church's name is The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. In 2018 Church leaders asked that Mormon not be used as a nickname for the Church or its members, to keep the name of Jesus Christ first.

Members still recognize Mormon as a historical and cultural word, taken from the Book of Mormon prophet-compiler. Many still use it in older books and in casual speech. Official preference is Latter-day Saint or member of the Church of Jesus Christ.
lds.true_church_claim:
Latter-day Saints claim that this Church is the restored Church of Jesus Christ, the only one on the earth that holds all the priesthood keys given in this dispensation. That is what they mean by the only true and living church.

The claim is about authority, ordinances, and continuing revelation. It is not a claim that God loves only this people, or that no truth exists elsewhere. Members are still taught to honor the good in other churches while inviting all to receive the restored fullness.
